title: The Venetian Diplomat Who Invented Quarantine
event_summary: The city council of Ragusa, led by rector Jacobus de Veneciis, passed a law called 'trentino' requiring all ships and travelers arriving from plague-infected areas to isolate on the nearby island of Mrkan or in the town of Cavtat for thirty days before entering the city. This was the first codified quarantine law in recorded history, predating Venice's more famous lazaretto by nearly a century. The policy was so effective at curbing plague deaths that the isolation period was later extended to forty days — 'quaranta giorni' — giving us the word 'quarantine.'
why_forgotten: Venice's larger political and cultural shadow meant its own later quarantine measures from 1423 received most historical credit, eclipsing Ragusa's pioneering statute. Ragusa itself was a small republic whose archives were damaged by earthquakes and changing rulers, and the event lacked the drama of plague narratives centered on mass death rather than bureaucratic prevention.
why_it_matters: Every modern quarantine protocol, from COVID-19 lockdowns to airport health screenings, traces its legal and conceptual DNA directly to this 1377 Ragusan statute. It established the radical principle that a state could restrict individual movement to protect collective health — a tension between liberty and public safety that remains one of the most contested issues in global governance today.
